analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying for life and tightens rules on the lobbying industry.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have imposed a lifetime lobbying ban on former Members of Congress and new restrictions on the lobbying industry, was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on June 3, 2014 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for the "revolving door" between Congress and lobbying. Former Senators and House members would be banned from lobbying Congress for life, instead of two years for senators and one year for House members. Former congressional staff would face a six-year waiting period instead of one. It would also stop members of Congress from hiring registered lobbyists who had lobbied them, force large lobbying firms to publicly list which former lawmakers and senior staffers they employ, and raise fines for breaking lobbying disclosure rules. The bill was sent to the Senate Homeland Security committee and never went any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and taxpayers. The bill's restrictions apply to the people who write the laws and the industries that pay to influence them, so the public gains more visibility into who is lobbying whom (a searchable public database, lobbyists.gov, plus disclosure of which former lawmakers each big lobbying firm employs) and reduced legal access-buying by former officeholders. Anyone who thinks legislation is steered by ex-officials collecting lobbying paychecks benefits from those exit ramps being closed or slowed.

how_it_helps.text: It makes the post-congressional lobbying ban permanent for former Senators, House Members, and elected congressional officers, so leaving office can no longer be the first step toward a K Street career selling access to former colleagues.

It stretches the cooling-off period for congressional staff, including personal, committee, and leadership staff, from one year to six years, closing the fast track by which senior aides trade staff positions for lobbying jobs.

It bars Members and committees from hiring a registered lobbyist with whom they have had substantial lobbying contact for six years, cutting off the practice of lobbying firms placing their people directly inside the offices they seek to influence.

It requires large lobbying firms to disclose annually which former Members and senior former staffers they employ or pay as consultants, and to post that list on a searchable public website, lobbyists.gov, so voters can see where their former representatives went.

It gives enforcement teeth: lobbying firms must report their revolving-door hires to the D.C. U.S. Attorney for oversight, and the maximum civil penalty for violating lobbying disclosure rules rises from $200,000 to $500,000.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on former members of Congress and senior staff, who would lose the most lucrative use of their connections, and on lobbying firms and the industries that hire them — defense contractors, financial firms, pharmaceutical companies, and others who rely on ex-lawmakers and ex-staffers as hired advocates. Congressional offices would also face a six-year bar on hiring lobbyists who had lobbied them, narrowing their hiring pool.

drawbacks.text: A lifetime ban on lobbying by former Members is far broader than the existing two-year (Senate) and one-year (House) bans, and critics of long bans argue such rules can push influence-peddling into unregistered consulting and 'shadow lobbying' that is harder to track than formal lobbying.

The six-year hiring ban could deprive congressional committees of policy expertise, and the bill itself allows the Senate and House ethics committees to waive the restriction for a 'compelling national need,' which could blunt the rule in practice.

The bill raises the civil penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000 but does not add new investigators or funding beyond a $100,000 authorization for the lobbyists.gov website, leaving enforcement dependent on existing offices like the D.C. U.S. Attorney.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but simple: ex-Members and senior staff would no longer be able to sell their access the day after leaving office, and the public could see who lobbying firms employ. The strongest objection is that the ban is blunt — a lifetime prohibition on lobbying for Members, and six-year bans that cover most senior staff, could deter qualified people from seeking congressional jobs or push influence-peddling into unregistered "shadow" channels that are harder to police than formal lobbying. Critics also note that restricted hires can be waived by the ethics committees for "compelling national need," an escape hatch that could swallow the rule. On balance, the bill targeted a well-documented abuse — former officials monetizing their connections — with tools Congress has used before at smaller scale, and the mechanisms (disclosure, penalties, an enforceable cooling-off period) are straightforward. It was never given a working committee markup, so the design was never tested or improved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Bennet of Colorado introduced the Close the Revolving Door Act of 2014 in the Senate on June 3, 2014, joined by Senator Jon Tester of Montana.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
The committee never held a hearing or markup, no other committee acted, and the bill was never brought to the Senate floor.
Only two senators cosponsored the bill, both Democrats, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill dead in committee.

The bill would have replaced the existing two-year (Senate) and one-year (House) lobbying bans with a lifetime ban for former Members and a six-year ban for senior congressional staff, barred hiring of registered lobbyists who had substantially lobbied an office for six years, created a public searchable lobbying database, and raised the maximum civil penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The lobbying industry and former members of Congress and senior staff who sell their connections: the rules that would have restricted them never took effect, and the two-year and one-year cooling-off periods remain unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats (Bennet and Tester) sponsored or cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-controlled Senate committee to which it was referred never acted on it either.

industries.note: The bill would have barred former Members and senior staff from joining them for life or six years, barred them from placing lobbyists into congressional offices they had lobbied, forced public disclosure of which ex-lawmakers they employ, and raised penalties for disclosure violations to $500,000. Because the bill died in committee, the industry kept operating under the far looser existing rules.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their senior staff (the revolving door itself)
industries.note: The bill would have taken away the standard post-office exit: a lifetime lobbying ban for Members and a six-year ban for high-paid and senior-titled staff, plus a six-year bar on hiring lobbyists they dealt with. The industry that buys their influence, and the officials who sell it, both lost nothing because the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Industries that rely heavily on lobbying (defense, finance, pharmaceuticals)
industries.note: These sectors depend on former Members and senior staff walking through the revolving door to represent them; a functioning ban would have made their access more expensive and less effective. The bill's failure preserved the status quo, in which congressional connections remain a purchasable asset.
